Dynamic IRT (ideal points that drift)

Source: R/svb.R
dynirt.Rd

The one-dimensional dynamic item response model of Martin and Quinn (2002), made for courts: a vote is cast when \(z_{jk} = -\alpha_k + \beta_k \theta_{j,t(k)} + \varepsilon_{jk} > 0\); the ideal points follow a random walk, \(\theta_{j,0} \sim N(e_0, E_0)\), \(\theta_{j,t} \sim N(\theta_{j,t-1}, \tau^2_j)\); \(\alpha_k \sim N(a_0, 1/A_0)\), \(\beta_k \sim N(b_0, 1/B_0)\). Each sweep draws the latent utilities, every case's \((\alpha, \beta)\), every justice's path by forward filtering and backward sampling and, when c0 and d0 are positive, the evolution variances from \(IG((c_0 + T)/2, (d_0 + SS)/2)\). A draw is reflected whenever the anchor member's mean ideal point is negative. The chain starts from the first principal component of the votes. Draws come from seed, as set.seed() takes it.

Usage

dynirt(
  votes,
  period,
  nsamp = 500,
  burn = 100,
  seed = 42,
  thin = 1,
  tau2 = 1,
  c0 = -1,
  d0 = -1,
  e0 = 0,
  E0 = 1,
  a0 = 0,
  A0 = 0.1,
  b0 = 0,
  B0 = 0.1,
  anchor = NULL
)

Arguments

votes

A member-by-vote matrix of 0/1 votes (-1/1 is read as 0/1), NA absent.

period

The period (term) of each vote, one per column.

nsamp

The draws kept; nsamp times the values kept per draw must be at most 67108864 (2^26).

burn

The sweeps discarded first; burn plus nsamp times thin must be at most 2147483647.

seed

The seed.

thin

Keep every thin-th sweep.

tau2

The evolution variance (its start when estimated).

c0, d0

The inverse-gamma prior of \(\tau^2\), held at tau2 unless both are positive.

e0, E0

The prior mean and variance of the first ideal point.

a0, A0

The prior mean and precision of \(\alpha\).

b0, B0

The prior mean and precision of \(\beta\).

anchor

NULL (the largest first principal component score) or the row kept on the positive side.

Value

A list of class dynirt: theta and sd (members by periods), alpha, beta, tau2, periods, nsamp and anchor.

References

Martin, A. D. and Quinn, K. M. (2002). Dynamic ideal point estimation via Markov chain Monte Carlo for the U.S. Supreme Court, 1953-1999. Political Analysis, 10(2), 134-153. doi:10.1093/pan/10.2.134

See also

Other scaling: amscal(), anchv(), anomin(), bamscl(), bbscal(), bmdsf(), bunfld(), cjrirt(), cmdsf(), cutlns(), dblctr(), dwnom(), indscl(), ipsrec(), irtem(), irtlik(), irtpst(), mdsfit(), mlsmu(), nmdsf(), nombt(), nomll(), nompr(), nomutl(), nrmvec(), optcls(), ordirt(), ordocl(), procrs(), scboot(), smacf(), smunf(), unfstr(), votagr(), wrdfsh()

Examples

# 12 simulated justices over three terms of 15 cases
set.seed(7)
period <- rep(1:3, each = 15)
walk <- function(s) s + cumsum(c(0, rnorm(2, 0, 0.3)))
truth <- t(sapply(rnorm(12), walk))
p <- pnorm(-rep(rnorm(45, 0, 0.5), each = 12) +
  rep(rnorm(45, 1.5, 0.5), each = 12) * truth[, period])
V <- matrix(rbinom(length(p), 1, p), 12)
f <- dynirt(V, period, nsamp = 100, burn = 50)
cor(as.numeric(f$theta), as.numeric(truth))
#> [1] 0.9013526
